utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Good morning to everyone in and around the courtroom. Madam Registrar, please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. This is case number IT-04-81-T, the Prosecutor versus Momcilo Perisic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I don't know if it's me, but I'm hearing B/C/S on my headphones, and I am on channel 4. Are the lines crossed somehow? Thank you so much. Could we have appearances for today, starting with the Prosecution, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Dan Saxon for the Prosecution, with my colleagues Salvatore Cannata, Barney Thomas, and Carmela Javier.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. And for the Defence?

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honour. Novak Lukic, Danijela Tasic, Chad Mair, Milos Androvic, Tina Drolec, and I'm Gregor Guy-Smith, for the Defence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Guy-Smith. Just before we call the next witness, one or two housekeeping matters, please. On the 3rd -- I beg your pardon, on the 4th of November, there is a Plenary at 1.00 in the afternoon. The hope at this stage is that that Plenary might end before quarter past 2.00, and we might be able to start our case at a quarter past 2.00. If, however, it takes a little longer, we might start a little late. It's just a warning. But just to say the start time on that day. Secondly, on the 5th of November, again, after approaching various Trial Chambers, we have been approached also to contribute to the Appeals Chamber request for a number of days to hear their cases, and we tried to resist but finally we had to give the 5th of November. So we will not sit at all on the 5th of November. Okay? Thank you very much. Yes, Mr. Saxon.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Your Honour, Mr. Thomas will call the next witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. Yes, thanks. Sorry, I didn't catch the name. I'm trying to look for it in the script.

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: Barney Thomas, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Barney Thomas. Thank you, Mr. Thomas.

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: Before I call Mr. Bell, he is the only witness that the Prosecution has set for today. He has an estimated time of evidence-in-chief of two hours, so it was intended that he take the entire day. However, Your Honours, there is a matter relating to him, as well as to other witnesses, that I'd like to raise in advance of calling him because it may affect the evidence that he's able to give, and it may affect, in fact, whether -- how far we're able to proceed with him today. His intended evidence as --

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Your Honours, this is probably appropriately dealt with in the absence of Mr. Bell. Following Your Honours' rulings yesterday on the video clips that we intended to lead through Mr. Bell, what remains to be covered by his evidence includes effectively general comments that he is able to make regarding the shelling and sniping of civilians and the general life of civilians in Sarajevo. His evidence is two-fold in that respect. Firstly, he describes that situation and, secondly, he will give evidence as to how that was being reported by the international media at the time. And that remains essentially the sole focus of his evidence today. The Prosecution's view, as has been -- as it has put on the record previously, is that it does not consider such general comments of shelling and sniping of civilians to be what has been termed "unscheduled incidents" in the context of the 73 bis ruling such that would require a motion for leave to call that evidence. However, the Defence has a different view, and it has advanced in its responses to the Bell and Wilson motions that were filed a position that such general comments are caught by the 73 bis ruling which is therefore engaged and that the Prosecution is required to file a motion if it wants to lead evidence of a general nature regarding the shelling and sniping of civilians. The question --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You are speaking to the filing of this morning?

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. So that takes me to this morning's filing. The Prosecution wanted to set out by its submission this morning its arguments in support of the proposition that the 73 bis ruling does not apply to such general comments. The Prosecution sees the resolution of that question as necessary, not only for the ability to lead Mr. Bell through his evidence but also in relation to several, if not many, witnesses who will be called before this Trial Chamber during the course of the trial. It's a matter that is of importance, obviously, in that respect. It goes directly towards not just the evidence that people are able to give but the ability of the Prosecution to properly schedule witnesses and have them here in sufficient time, because if a four-week rule is going to operate in terms of even general comments about the shelling and sniping of civilians in Sarajevo, then that obviously causes -- that's something that the Prosecution needs to build in to its ability to present witnesses before the Trial Chamber on a timely basis. But our immediate concern this morning, sir, is that Mr. Bell will give that evidence and the question, therefore, arises as to how we deal with that, given that there remains this outstanding question. The Prosecution felt it was important to properly articulate its position, and therefore the submission has been filed, but I'm conscious of the fact, of course, Your Honour, that the Trial Chamber has only just received it and my learned friends have only just received it. And even though they have previously articulated their position in response to the proposition, perhaps you need to hear from my learned friends as to -- as to whether or not they are in a position or not to proceed with this question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Sure. I beg your pardon. Before I turn to your learned friends, can I get clarity on your position. When you filed the motion about which a decision was rendered yesterday, what was your understanding of unscheduled incidents?

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: In terms of general comments relating to the shelling and sniping generally of civilians, Your Honour, our proposition, our position, always was that we did not consider such general comments to be caught by the decision, and we footnoted that position in those two motions. The position we take on the submission has altered a little, in fact, from the position that we took at the time of filing of the motions in respect of General Wilson. I should stress, Your Honour, that the submission is not an attempt in any way to relitigate the Wilson motion. That is done and the decision has been rendered. The motions themselves had their genesis in the issues that arose during the examination of Mr. van Lynden on the first day of testimony in the trial where incidents that we hadn't anticipated would amount to unscheduled incidents became the subject of discussion in this court, and we were aware at that time that we had scheduled Bell, or were intending to schedule Mr. Bell, and General Wilson to give evidence this week, and we were concerned that we did not want to run into any arguments or any objections at the last minute in relation to Mr. Bell and General Wilson, should incidents, if I can describe them generally in that way, be categorised as unscheduled incidents which would require leave and a motion to be filed. So it was that which prompted the motions in respect of Mr. Bell and General Wilson. In relation to General Wilson, the specific incidents which were pleaded in that motion related to shelling in the period of May to June 1992. As I've said, Your Honour, that was primarily motivated by a concern that we not fly General Wilson from Australia all the way here to be present in the witness box and to meet an objection that that constituted an unscheduled incident or not. The Prosecution, having filed its submission overnight, has examined once again the process by which the Trial -- the Pre-Trial Chamber game to its decision in the 73 bis ruling and how it came to draw a distinction between scheduled incidents and unscheduled incidents, and the Prosecution is of the view, which it has set out in its submission, that, in fact, even those Wilson incidents would not be characterised by that Pre-Trial Chamber as unscheduled incidents requiring leave. But that, as I've said, Your Honour, is something that -- a position that have been arrived at subsequent to the filing of that motion, and that's -- I'm not intending to re-open that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: But I indicate that because there is specific reference to that in the submission, because that is the very part of the pre-trial brief that the Pre-Trial Chamber referred to in its decision.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I am not quite sure I have followed you quite clearly. Do I understand you to be saying, in one sentence, that general comments on shelling and sniping in Sarajevo, in the view of the Prosecution, should not be caught by the term "scheduled incidents"?

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: It should not be caught by the term "scheduled --" "unscheduled incidents," which would require leave.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Right. Now, in the view of the Prosecution, what, then, are those unscheduled incidents which would then require leave?

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: When one goes back to the particularly footnoted passages of the 73 bis decision which deal with references in the pre-trial brief, which deal with the Prosecution's amended witness list, which included the 65 ter witness summaries, the Prosecution's position is that the term "unscheduled incident," as considered by the Pre-Trial Chamber, amounts to those incidents which are usually expressly described as such in the 65 ter witness summaries, and annexed to the submission -- sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Described as "scheduled incidents" in the 65 ter list.

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: In the 65 ter summaries, Your Honour, one of which is annexed to the submission by way of example. Some witnesses are being called to give evidence about scheduled incidents. There is a heading "Scheduled Incident A7," and then it sets out what that witness is intending to say about that particular scheduled incident. In the same summary, there will also be, under usually a separate heading, an unscheduled incident, "Unscheduled Incident, 2nd May, 1994" where the witness -- and then a passage dealing with the witness's intended evidence regarding that particular unscheduled incident. There are on some occasions isolated instances in the 65 ter summaries where those unscheduled incidents do not appear under a separate heading in the 65 ter summary, but at the end of the summary where the particular relevance of the witness's evidence is set out, there is reference to that particular unscheduled incident. In other words, if I can put it concisely, Your Honour, the Prosecution's position in relation to what the Pre-Trial Chamber meant when it was talking about unscheduled incidents requiring leave is those which are expressly identified as such in the -- in the 65 ter summaries.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Guy-Smith.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: If I could, for the moment, I have not had the opportunity to review the Prosecution's submission, but I would like to have the opportunity to do that, obviously, and I don't think that Mr. Thomas is taking any exception to that. He's really trying to work out where we go from here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: There is one quick thought that comes to mind based upon what Mr. Thomas has said with regard to a definition of "unscheduled incidents," and I refer the Chamber and Counsel to paragraph 11 of the decision, which has oftentimes been cited to you, concerning the 73 bis matter, specifically paragraph -- the second sentence in paragraph 11, which probably should be read in context of the first. "After hearing the Prosecutor," this is the first sentence, paragraph 11, "the Chamber may reduce the number of counts charged and fix on the basis of the criteria set out in Rule 73 bis (D) of the rules crime sites or incidents that are 'reasonably representative of the crimes charged' and for which evidence will be presented," which they have done in scheduled incidents. The second sentence, I think, is of some importance in the analysis, no matter when we really grapple with the entirety of the issue. "The corollary of fixing the number of crime sites or incidents in respect of which evidence will be presented is that," and now I emphasise, "the Prosecution shall not present evidence in respect of other crime sites or incidents that are not included in the fixed number." Now, I think that, when read in conjunction with the analysis that we have gone through on a number of occasions in paragraph 16 and 17, answer the question in a relatively clear manner, and I don't think there is any dispute or room for, as the Prosecution has suggested, interpretation of what that means. However, that does not deal with, certainly, some of the procedural as well as substantive issues that still are to be addressed with regard to this whole area, and specifically the analysis that is engaged in by the Chamber in paragraph 17. Having said that, I would like to stop for the moment and ask for the opportunity to read the submission and see how best to respond in a cogent and comprehensive manner to it. But I thought I should just mention that in passing, because it may quickly take care of the issue because it wasn't addressed by the Prosecution in their submission just now, and it seems to be avoided in terms of what the Chamber has done with regard to the specific matter in hand and that is the definition of "incidents." But I need some -- I need some time in addition if that doesn't settle the issue at first blush.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Guy-Smith. Let me just make one or two comments. I find myself, and I want to believe that I'm speaking on behalf of my fellow Judges, if I say that we are equally a little at sea about this matter because we are -- we only saw the filing this morning. We haven't read it. Certainly, I haven't read it. And I don't feel that I'm sufficiently informed to be able to make a contribution towards a decision. But just one question that I would like to ask you, Mr. Guy-Smith, from this quotation that you have just given us, you said that "the Prosecution shall not present evidence in respect of other crime sites or incidents that are not included in the fixed number." Is that a fixed number of incidents that constitute, according to that decision, that constitute scheduled incidents, and can one sort of go somewhere and find it?

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: That's how I have understood the decision, and in response to your question, what I then did is I went to the indictment and went to the schedules following -- following the indictment that had a fixed number of identified incidents; for example, schedules A and B, which are really what the subject matter is we are talking about. Schedule A has nine incidents; schedule B has 12 incidents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Well, that's the simplistic approach that I was taking to this matter insofar as the definition of "scheduled" and "unscheduled incidents" refers. I was looking at the schedules to the indictment.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: You and I were doing the same thing, Your Honour. That's what I understood to be the fixed number that they're talking about. That's where I went. I went from paragraph 11 to the indictment, I saw what was here. I then took a look at the analysis in paragraph 16 and 17 to see where there could be any deviation and how the deviation -- and if there could be deviation from those incidents, how that occurred. And that led me to an understanding of what the -- what the Chamber's analysis was there, which is that "thou," meaning the Prosecution, "shall not lead evidence on --" what now is being called - and I think is being used euphemistically, to be perfectly honest with you - is now being called "general conditions," and I think what they really mean there is precisely what the Chamber said they should not do, which is lead evidence on terror in relation to the Sarajevo counts. I think it's pretty clear what this evidence is about. I then went to paragraph 17 and understood from paragraph 17 that there were two predicates that had to be met in order for an unscheduled incident to be considered by the Chamber to be allowed to be led. One was the issue of notice; that's the procedural matter. And the second is the substantive matter, and the substantive matter had to tie in to a particular requirement that it proved an essential aspect of the case, and then they gave an example, which is the same example -- and I don't mean to be repetitive, because I seem to be just repeating that which the decision says, and it says, "... if a scheduled incident is necessary to link the accused to the crimes charged." I think the decision is pretty straightforward. I was not having the difficulty in interpretation that the Prosecution was which didn't mean that our job is -- of the Defence was any easier. We still had a formidable task in front of us to counter the evidence that the Prosecution planned on bringing, but it seemed that the analysis that the Chamber had gone through was pretty clear. There was sufficient evidence in the crimes that were charged and the incidents related to those crimes that allowed for the concern that the Prosecution had concerning notice, as well as other aspects that they must prove. And in the event there was something above and beyond, something special, something extraordinary, then they would come to the Chamber and ask for leave, after having made a good showing both in terms of a procedural reason why they had failed to bring this up at any earlier time as well as a substantive reason. That was the way that I was interpreting and have been consistently interpreting this decision, as has my colleague. And to a certain extent, I don't think that there's been a dissimilar approach in analysis in some of the conversations that have been had as between the parties. I think it's more a question of preference of how to present the evidence in this case as opposed to that which is essential for proof in this case. I'll leave it at that because conversations as between the parties oftentimes are subject to interpretation that may be different as between us, and I don't want to push that particularly hard. I hope that I've -- I looked at this as a pretty straightforward ruling. I didn't see too much -- I didn't see too much ambiguity here. And perhaps I'm not as nuanced as others, but I just didn't see it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Can I just find out from you, Mr. Guy-Smith, while you're on your feet, would you include annex -- I beg your pardon, schedule C amongst the scheduled incidents, in your understanding?

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Absolutely. I mean, anything that's scheduled -- anything that's here that's scheduled is -- I would include.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Thomas, I'm sure you're aware of the dilemma in which we have all landed.

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You've told us that Mr. Bell comes from Australia --

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: No, he's from the UK, sir. He's -- rescheduling him, if necessary, doesn't present difficulties. It's General Wilson who comes from Australia, and he's here tomorrow, but that's -- so our difficulty today just involves Mr. Bell. He's from the UK.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: But you realise that, having not read your filing this morning, the Defence having not had an opportunity to respond, we are -- we cannot be in a position to give a decision. In fact, I'm not quite sure I've been able to digest your arguments this morning. I would like to hear them again, and maybe after reading the submission, then I might be able to follow what you're saying better.

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: And my question is what, then, what we do with Mr. Bell, who is standing outside ready to testify?

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: This is why I wanted to raise this in advance, sir. I don't see, in the absence of a ruling, given the positions taken by the parties, that we can deal with Mr. Bell's evidence. My learned friends still dispute that the general comments that he would make about shelling and sniping of civilians constitutes or don't constitute an unscheduled incident, and while they take that position, that's something that would have to be resolved before he's able to give that evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: On the way forward, there are two -- it looks to me like there are two options here, and I put them to the parties to make a recommendation to the Bench. Either we adjourn for the day and make sure that this matter is properly ventilated and a properly reasoned decision is rendered or, in trying to accommodate Mr. Bell, we hear Mr. Bell on whatever it is that the Prosecution wants to lead on the understanding that once this matter has been properly ventilated at a later stage and depending on the decision that is rendered, whatever needs to be expunged from Mr. Bell's testimony as not being scheduled incident shall be expunged. I'm not sure whether that second alternative came out clearly. Yes, Mr. Thomas -- you are on your feet.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I believe I understood the second alternative quite well. If it's not too much of an imposition on the Court, if the Prosecution and the Defence could talk for a moment, perhaps we could address the issue, because, as I understand it, Mr. Bell is -- Mr. Bell is waiting outside. I have no desire to inconvenience him whatsoever.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: That's an alternative. That's a third alternative.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: If we could have a moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Would you prefer that, Mr. Thomas?

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: I'd certainly appreciate the opportunity to consider the matter just briefly for a moment, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: That's quite okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The parties will notify us when they are ready to start?

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay. We'll take an adjournment. --- Break taken at 9.36 a.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Thomas.

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: Sir, I can -- Your Honours, I can advise that my learned friends and I have been discussing the matter. We agree that the greatest importance in so much as we are able to influence that should be placed upon resolving the issue and obtaining a decision. This is an issue that affects not just Mr. Bell but also Mr. Wilson and probably all of the international witnesses in some limited form or another. My learned friends and I are both happy, as is Mr. Bell, if it would assist the Court, for him to travel back on another occasion. We are certainly, both I and my friends, of the view that Mr. Bell shouldn't give his evidence until there is a ruling on what can be -- what should be the compass of his evidence, and the same would apply to General Wilson. I'm conscious, of course, Your Honours, that both the Trial Chamber and my learned friends haven't had and need the opportunity to proper consider the Prosecution's submission. Mr. Bell, if he's not going to testify today, can come back on another occasion. That is not a problem. I'm awaiting confirmation almost at any minute that General Wilson is here and would be available to give evidence Monday, perhaps even Tuesday of next week, if my learned friends needed more time to be able to address these issues, for example, tomorrow, instead of today. In any event, the lesser of two evils would probably be, as far as the Prosecution is concerned, that General Wilson give his testimony after such a decision, even if that means he has to return sometime in the future. But my learned friends and I are in agreement that this is a -- this is a decision that will dictate how many witnesses are going to be dealt with. It shouldn't affect in terms of timing anything too significant. But because a lot of witnesses are going to be commenting in some way on these issues, that my learned friends and I both feel that we should spend the time resolving the issue, getting the decision, before evidence of this type is led.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Thomas. Mr. Guy-Smith.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: We agree.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You're agreed. And the sum total is we adjourn.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: That would be our joint request at this time, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Before we do so, how --

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: How soon can we get something on file or be in a position to respond? If I could have two seconds.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I'll give you five.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Your Honour, if I could just interrupt for a moment. I've just received notification that General Wilson --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Has arrived.

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: He's here. He would be amenable -- well, his arrangements allow him to testify on Monday or "a few days later, if necessary," or he's able to return sometime in the future as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you very much, Mr. Thomas. Yes, Mr. Guy-Smith. That, I hope, doesn't affect the timeline for your filing?

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: No, it doesn't. I'd like to say maybe grab an hour or two more, but other than that, no. If we could -- if we could have -- today is Wednesday. If we could have the balance of the day and perhaps get some in file first thing tomorrow morning, that would be appreciated.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I think we can work within that timeframe.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Sure. I think that should take care of the issue about scheduling. I think it should give us enough time, I would think.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes. I'm trying to think whether -- if you're going to file tomorrow morning, it doesn't seem to make sense to postpone to tomorrow morning, because we'll only get your filing tomorrow morning, and then we'll need to consider it --

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: -- and draft our decision. Most probably -- you said today's Wednesday?

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Sorry, Judge Picard just pointed out to me that yes, we don't sit on Fridays. So if we can't sit tomorrow, then it can only be Monday.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Very well, then. The matter stands postponed to Monday -- sorry, Judge. Let me just check the dates. Monday, the 3rd of November, at quarter past 2.00 in the afternoon. It will be in Courtroom II. Thank you very much. Court adjourned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Monday, the 3rd day of November, 2008, at 2.15 p.m. 24

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 10.14 a.m.,
